                 Defendants.                          INJUNCTION
                                                      Re: Dkt. Nos. 16, 18



       The court has reviewed de novo Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixson’s Report and

Recommendation Re: Motion for Default Judgment (Dkt. No. 18, “R&R”), as well as the Motion

and associated exhibits (Dkt. No. 16), the executed returns of the summons (Dkt. Nos. 8 & 9),

Plaintiff Meta Platform Inc.’s request for clarification regarding the Report and Recommendation

(Dkt. No. 22), and the docket in the matter. No objections have been received to the R&R from

Defendants. The Court finds the R&R correct, well-reasoned and thorough, and adopts it in its
entirety, with the clarification that Meta’s suit is to enforce “the Instagram Terms of Use . . . and

other rules that govern access to and use of Instagram, including Instagram’s Community

Standards,” and not Meta’s “Commercial Terms.” (See id.)

       Accordingly, Meta’s Motion for Default Judgment is GRANTED. Defendants Idriss

Qibaa and Unlocked4Life, LLC, and any of their agents, servants, employers, successors, and

assigns, and all other persons acting in concert or conspiring with any of them or who are

affiliated with Defendants, are PERMANENTLY ENJOINED and RESTRAINED from:
       a) Accessing, attempting to access, or using Meta’s services, platforms, or computer



                                                  1
        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL          Document 23        Filed 08/29/25      Page 2 of 2




          systems, including Instagram or Facebook, for any purpose whatsoever;

       b) Creating or maintaining any Instagram accounts in violation of the Instagram Terms

          of Use;

       c) Engaging in any activity or facilitating others to do the same that violates the

          Instagram Terms of Use;

       d) Soliciting third parties to access Meta’s platforms or computer systems on

          Defendants’ behalf;

       e) Engaging in any activity that disrupts, diminishes the quality of, interferes with the

          performance of, or impairs the functionality of Meta’s computers, computer system,

          or computer network or service; and

       f) Engaging in any activity that violates the California Comprehensive Computer Data

          Access and Fraud Act (California Penal Code § 502).

       If Meta intends to seek attorneys’ fees and costs, it must make its request by separate

motion with supporting evidence, by September 11, 2025. See Local Civ. R. 54-1(a).



       IT IS SO ORDERED.

Dated: August 28, 2025




                                                             RITA F. LIN
                                                             United States District Judge

                                  15                                        III.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                  16            Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 55(b)(2) permits a court, following default by a defendant,

                                  17   to enter default judgment in a case. “The district court’s decision whether to enter default

                                  18   judgment is a discretionary one.” Aldabe v. Aldabe, 616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980).

                                  19            At the default judgment stage, the factual allegations of the complaint, except those

                                  20   concerning damages, “together with other competent evidence submitted” are deemed admitted by

                                  21   the non-responding parties. Shanghai Automation Instrument Co. v. Kuei, 194 F. Supp. 2d 995,

                                  22   1000 (N.D. Cal. 2001); see also Fair Hous. of Marin v. Combs, 285 F.3d 899, 906 (9th Cir. 2002)

                                       release. Id., ECF No. 57.

                                  18                                            IV.    DISCUSSION
                                  19   A.     Jurisdiction and Service of Process
                                  20          In considering whether to enter default judgment, a district court must first determine

                                  21   whether it has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties to the case. In re Tuli, 172 F.3d

                                  22   707, 712 (9th Cir. 1999). “[T]he district court is not restricted to the face of the pleadings, but

                                  23   may review any evidence, such as affidavits and testimony, to resolve factual disputes concerning

                                  24   the existence of jurisdiction.” McCarthy v. United States, 850 F.2d 558, 560 (9th Cir. 1988)

                                  25   (considering subject matter jurisdiction on a 12(b)(1) motion).

                                  26          1.      Subject Matter Jurisdiction
                                  27          Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction and are presumptively without jurisdiction.

                                  28   Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375, 377 (1994). A federal court may
                                                                                          7
                                         Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL           Document 18          Filed 08/01/25    Page 8 of 18




                                   1   dismiss an action on its own motion if it finds that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction. Fiedler v.

                                   2   Clark, 714 F.2d 77, 78-79 (9th Cir. 1983); see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(3) (“If the court

                                   3   determines at any time that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, the court must dismiss the

                                   4   action.”). The Court has diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 because Meta is in

                                   5   California, Defendants are in Nevada, and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. Compl. ¶¶

                                   6   4–6, 9; see Naffe v. Frey, 789 F.3d 1030, 1039 (9th Cir. 2015) (“To establish federal jurisdiction

                                   7   under § 1332(a)(1), the proponent must allege (1) the parties are completely diverse, and (2) the

                                   8   amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.”).

                                   9          2.      Personal Jurisdiction
                                  10          To enter default judgment, the Court must have a basis for the exercise of personal

                                  11   jurisdiction over the defendants in default. In re Tuli, 172 F.3d at 712. “Without a proper basis

                                  12   for [personal] jurisdiction, or in the absence of proper service of process, the district court has no
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   power to render any judgment against the defendant’s person or property unless the defendant has

                                  14   consented to jurisdiction or waived the lack of process.” S.E.C. v. Ross, 504 F.3d 1130, 1138-39

                                  15   (9th Cir. 2007). Traditional bases for conferring a court with personal jurisdiction include a

                                  16   defendant’s consent to jurisdiction, personal service of the defendant within the forum state, or a

                                  17   defendant’s citizenship or domicile in the forum state. J. McIntyre Mach., Ltd. v. Nicastro, 564

                                  18   U.S. 873, 880 (2011).

                                  19          A defendant may consent to a court’s personal jurisdiction through a forum selection

                                  20   clause, provided the defendant “agrees to be so bound.” Holland Am. Line Inc. v. Wartsila N. Am.,

                                  21   Inc., 485 F.3d 450, 458 (9th Cir. 2007) (citations omitted). Forum selection clauses are to be

                                  22   specifically enforced unless the party opposing the clause clearly shows “that enforcement would

                                  23   be unreasonable and unjust, or that the clause was invalid for such reasons as fraud or

                                  24   overreaching.” Manetti-Farrow, Inc. v. Gucci Am., Inc., 858 F.2d 509, 512 (9th Cir. 1988)

                                  25   (internal quotation and citation omitted). “Courts routinely uphold forum selection clauses in

                                  26   form contracts between consumers and businesses.” Thomas v. Facebook, Inc., 2018 WL

                                  27   3915585, at *4 (E.D. Cal. Aug. 15, 2018) (citing Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute, 499 U.S.

                                  28   585, 587 (1991)).

                                  22   B.     Eitel Factors
                                  23          Applying the seven Eitel factors, the undersigned finds default judgment is warranted in

                                  24   favor of Meta.

                                  25          1.        The Possibility of Prejudice
                                  26          The first factor the Court considers is the possibility of prejudice if a default judgment is

                                  27   not entered. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471-72. This factor weighs in favor of default judgment “when a

                                  28   defendant has failed to appear or defend against a suit, and the plaintiffs could not otherwise seek
                                                                                         9
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL          Document 18        Filed 08/01/25      Page 10 of 18




                                   1   relief.” Vietnam Reform Party v. Viet Tan – Vietnam Reform Party, 416 F. Supp. 3d 948, 962

                                   2   (N.D. Cal. 2019) (citations omitted); IO Grp., Inc. v. Jordon, 708 F. Supp. 2d 989, 997 (N.D. Cal.

                                   3   2010) (prejudice exists where denying the requested default judgment would leave the plaintiff

                                   4   without a proper remedy). Because Defendants have not appeared in this action, Meta will be

                                   5   unable to prevent Defendants from further violating its Terms or engaging in other disruptive

                                   6   conduct unless the Court grants its motion. This fact favors granting default judgment under the

                                   7   first Eitel factor. See Nguyen, 2023 WL 8686924, at *6 (default judgment proper where Meta

                                   8   would otherwise be unable to prevent defendants from further violating its Terms).

                                  13   recover.’” Vietnam Reform Party, 416 F. Supp. 3d at 962 (quoting PepsiCo, Inc. v. Cal. Sec.

                                  14   Cans, 238 F. Supp. 2d 1172, 1175 (C.D. Cal. 2002)). “Of all the Eitel factors, courts often

                                  15   consider the second and third factors to be ‘the most important.’” Id. (quoting Sanrio, Inc. v. Jay

                                  16   Yoon, 2012 WL 610451, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 24, 2012)).

                                  17                  a.      Breach of Contract
                                  18          Under California law, the “cause of action for damages for breach of contract is comprised

                                  19   of the following elements: (1) the contract, (2) plaintiff’s performance or excuse for

                                  20   nonperformance, (3) defendant’s breach, and (4) the resulting damages to plaintiff.” Armstrong

                                  21   Petroleum Corp. v. Tri-Valley Oil & Gas Co., 116 Cal. App. 4th 1375, 1391 n.6 (2004).

                                  22          First, valid contracts exist between Meta and Defendants. “Defendants agreed to the . . .

                                  23   Instagram Terms of Service and Use by accessing, creating, and using . . . Instagram accounts.”

                                  24   Meta Platforms, Inc. v. Arowokoko, 2023 WL 3035454, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 24, 2023), report

                                  25   and recommendation adopted, 2023 WL 4013626 (N.D. Cal. May 9, 2023) (collecting cases

                                  26   involving Facebook, Yelp, and Craigslist); see Compl. ¶¶ 17, 22–23; Andre Decl. ¶ 3, ECF No.

                                  27   16-2 (“Meta owns and operates several products, including Instagram. Every user who registers

                                  28   for, uses, and continues to use Instagram must agree to Instagram’s Terms and Policies.”). The
                                                                                        10
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL          Document 18        Filed 08/01/25    Page 11 of 18




                                   1   Terms prohibit users from doing anything unlawful, misleading, or fraudulent or for an illegal or

                                   2   unauthorized purpose. Compl. ¶ 18. The Terms also prohibit accessing or attempting to access

                                   3   accounts in unauthorized ways; doing anything to interfere with or impair the intended operation

                                   4   of Instagram; and misusing any reporting, dispute, or appeals channel. Id. ¶¶ 19–20. And the

                                   5   Terms prohibit someone from using Instagram if Meta has previously disabled that person’s user

                                   6   account for violating any law or Meta’s policies. Id. ¶¶ 21, 51.

                                   7          Second, Meta performed its end of the bargain by “allowing Defendants to use . . .

                                   8   Instagram, until Meta became aware that they were in breach of the . . . Instagram Terms.”

                                   9   Arowokoko, 2023 WL 3035454, at *7; see Compl. ¶¶ 23, 28–40.

                                  10          Third, Defendants breached the Terms by offering for sale and selling unauthorized

                                  11   Instagram services including services to disable Instagram user accounts; misusing Meta

                                  12   reporting, dispute, or appeal channels in furtherance of their scheme; and creating multiple new
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Instagram accounts and continuing to use Instagram accounts after Meta sent the cease-and-desist

                                  14   letter informing Defendants they were no longer authorized to access Instagram. See Arowokoko,

                                  15   2023 WL 3035454, at *7 (finding breach where defendants mislead and defrauded users, including

                                  16   by creating multiple Facebook accounts and continuing to use Facebook after Meta disabled their

                                  17   accounts for violating the Facebook Terms and continuing to use Instagram after Meta disabled

                                  18   their account for violating the Instagram Terms); Compl. ¶¶ 28–45, 50–51.

                                  19          Finally, as a result of Defendants’ actions, Meta suffered damages. Compl. ¶ 52. Among

                                  20   other things, Meta expended resources to investigate, remediate, and respond to Defendants’

                                  21   breaching conduct. Id.; see Arowokoko, 2023 WL 3035454, at *8 (finding damages where Meta

                                  22   alleged it had incurred damages “in excess of $75,000, including for significant time and expense

                                  23   spent investigating and taking enforcement actions against Defendants”) (citing Speirs v. BlueFire

                                  24   Ethanol Fuels, Inc., 243 Cal. App. 4th 969, 989 (2015)); Facebook, Inc. v. 9 Xiu Network

                                  25   (Shenzhen) Tech. Co., Ltd., 2021 WL 5707741, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 21, 2021), report and

                                  26   recommendation adopted, 2021 WL 5707740 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 16, 2021) (Meta sufficiently pled

                                  27   damages element of contract claim by alleging that it had to “expend time and resources to

                                  28   investigate” and remediate prohibited activities); Facebook, Inc. v. Sluchevsky, 2020 WL 5823277,
                                                                                        11

                                   1   at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 28, 2020), report and recommendation adopted, 2020 WL 5816578 (N.D.

                                   2   Cal. Sept. 30, 2020) (same).

                                   3             Accordingly, the undersigned finds Meta has established its breach of contract claim.

                                   4                    b.     California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act
                                   5             The CDAFA prohibits the unauthorized access and use of any data from a computer,

                                   6   computer system, or computer network. Cal. Penal Code § 502. “Section 502 is an anti-hacking

                                   7   statute intended to prohibit the unauthorized use of any computer system for improper or

                                   8   illegitimate purpose.” Sunbelt Rentals, Inc. v. Victor, 43 F. Supp. 3d 1026, 1032 (N.D. Cal. 2014).

                                   9   The Ninth Circuit has held that continued use of Meta’s services after receipt of a cease-and-desist

                                  10   letter violates Section 502. Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058, 1069 (9th Cir.

                                  11   2016) (“[W]hen Facebook sent the cease and desist letter, Power, as it conceded, knew that it no

                                  12   longer had permission to access Facebook’s computers at all. Power, therefore, knowingly
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   accessed and without permission took, copied, and made use of Facebook’s data.”); see also Meta

                                  14   Platforms, Inc. v. Ates, 2023 WL 4035611, at *6 (N.D. Cal. May 1, 2023), report and

                                  15   recommendation adopted, 2023 WL 4995717 (N.D. Cal. June 27, 2023) (“The Ninth Circuit has

                                  16   held that continued use of Meta’s services after receipt of a cease-and-desist letter violates section

                                  17   502.”); Rodriguez v. Google LLC, 772 F. Supp. 3d 1093, 1107 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (“The Ninth

                                  18   Circuit held that previously permitted use runs afoul of the CFAA (and therefore the CDAFA)

                                  19   ‘when such permission has been revoked explicitly.’”) (quoting Power Ventures, 844 F.3d at

                                  20   1069)).

                                  21             Here, Defendants accessed and used Instagram to promote their unauthorized services after

                                  22   Meta sent them a cease-and-desist letter and revoked their access to Instagram on February 9,

                                  23   2024. See Compl. ¶¶ 40–45. Accordingly, the undersigned finds Meta has established its CDAFA

                                  24   claim.

                                  25             3.     The Sum of Money at Stake in the Action
                                  26             Under the fourth Eitel factor, “the Court must consider the amount of money at stake in

                                  27   relation to the seriousness of Defendant’s conduct.” Dr. JKL Ltd., v. HPC IT Educ. Ctr., 749 F.

                                  28   Supp. 2d 1038, 1050 (N.D. Cal. 2010) (citation and quotation marks omitted). When the amount
                                                                                         12
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL            Document 18        Filed 08/01/25      Page 13 of 18




                                   1   at stake is substantial or unreasonable in light of the allegations in the complaint, default judgment

                                   2   is disfavored. See Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1472 (affirming the denial of default judgment where the

                                   3   plaintiff sought $3 million in damages and the parties disputed material facts in the pleadings).

                                   4   “However, when the sum of money at stake is tailored to the specific misconduct of the defendant,

                                   5   default judgment may be appropriate.” Yelp Inc. v. Catron, 70 F. Supp. 3d 1082, 1100 (N.D. Cal.

                                   6   2014).

                                   7            Here, as Meta seeks injunctive relief and attorneys’ fees and costs only, this factor favors

                                   8   granting default judgment. See Sluchevsky, 2020 WL 5823277, at *8 (finding the “fourth Eitel

                                   9   factor weigh[ed] in favor of granting the plaintiff’s motion” when the plaintiff sought only

                                  10   injunctive relief and attorneys’ fees and costs) (citing MERSCORP Holdings, Inc. v. MERS, Inc.,

                                  11   2017 WL 1709351, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 3, 2017)).

                                  12            4.     The Possibility of Dispute Concerning Material Facts
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            The fifth Eitel factor examines the likelihood of dispute between the parties regarding the

                                  14   material facts surrounding the case. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471-72. However, upon entry of default,

                                  15   the defendant is “deemed to have admitted all well-pleaded factual allegations” in the complaint.

                                  16   DIRECTV, Inc., 503 F.3d at 851 (citing Fed. R. Civ. P. 55(a)). Moreover, as outlined above, Meta

                                  17   has provided the Court with well-pleaded allegations supporting its claims. Accordingly, this

                                  18   factor weighs in favor of default judgment.

                                  19            5.     Whether Default was Due to Excusable Neglect
                                  20            The sixth Eitel factor examines whether the defendant’s failure to respond to the complaint

                                  21   was the result of excusable neglect. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471-72. Here, despite being properly

                                  22   served with the summons and complaint and entry of default at email addresses known to be used

                                  23   by them, Defendants have “made no appearance in this [action].” Yelp Inc., 70 F. Supp. 3d at

                                  24   1100. Nothing in the record suggests Defendants had an excusable reason for failing to appear.

                                  25            6.     Policy Favoring Deciding a Case on its Merits
                                  26            The last Eitel factor examines whether the policy of deciding a case based on the merits

                                  27   precludes entry of default judgment. Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1472. In Eitel, the Ninth Circuit

                                  28   admonished that “[c]ases should be decided on their merits whenever reasonably possible.” Id.
                                                                                          13
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL          Document 18        Filed 08/01/25      Page 14 of 18




                                   1   “The existence of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 55(b), however, shows that this policy is not

                                   2   dispositive.” McMillan Data Commc’ns, Inc. v. AmeriCom Automation Servs., Inc., 2015 WL

                                   3   4380965, at *11 (N.D. Cal. July 16, 2015) (citing Kloepping v. Fireman’s Fund, 1996 WL 75314,

                                   4   at *3 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 13, 1996)). Further, “deciding the case on the merits is impossible where a

                                   5   party refuses to participate.” Vietnam Reform Party, 416 F. Supp. 3d at 970. Thus, because

                                   6   Defendants made no effort to respond to communication attempts by Meta and in no way

                                   7   participated in the proceedings, “[t]his factor thus weighs against, but does not preclude, entry of

                                   8   default judgment.” Id.

                                   9          7.      Summary of the Eitel Factors
                                  10          In sum, the majority of the Eitel factors weigh in favor of granting default judgment.

                                  11   Accordingly, the undersigned RECOMMENDS the District Court GRANT the motion and enter

                                  12   default judgment against Defendants.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   C.     Relief Sought
                                  14          The Court next turns to the relief Meta seeks. Once liability is established, the plaintiff

                                  15   must then establish that the requested relief is appropriate. Geddes v. United Fin. Grp., 559 F.2d

                                  16   557, 560 (9th Cir. 1977). A “default judgment must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount,

                                  17   what is demanded in the pleadings.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(c).

                                  18          1.      Attorneys’ Fees and Costs
                                  19          Meta requests the attorneys’ fees associated with its pre-filing investigation of Defendants,

                                  20   filing and service of the complaint, and pursuit of Defendants’ default and default judgment. Mot.

                                  21   at 22. California Penal Code section 502 permits a prevailing party to recover attorneys’ fees.

                                  22   Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(2) (“In any action brought pursuant to this subdivision the court may

                                  23   award reasonable attorney's fees.”); see, e.g., Sluchevsky, 2020 WL 5823277, at *10; Facebook,

                                  24   Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 2017 WL 3394754, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 8, 2017). Accordingly, the

                                  25   undersigned RECOMMENDS the Court grant Meta’s request for attorneys’ fees and costs, which

                                  26   Meta states it will establish by separate motion and supporting evidence following resolution of

                                  27   this motion.

                                  28

                                   1           2.      Injunctive Relief

                                   2           Meta also seeks injunctive relief, which is authorized under the CDAFA. See Cal. Penal

                                   3   Code § 502(e)(1). Meta is also entitled to injunctive relief for its breach of contract claim under

                                   4   California law. See Arowokoko, 2023 WL 3035454, at *9; Twitch Interactive, Inc. v. Johnston,

                                   5   2019 WL 3387977, at *12 (N.D. Cal. July 26, 2019) (citing DVD Copy Control Ass'n, Inc. v.

                                   6   Kaleidescape, Inc., 176 Cal. App. 4th 697, 721–23 (2009)). Meta seeks an order restraining

                                   7   Defendants from: (a) accessing and using Meta’s services, platforms, and computer systems; (b)

                                   8   creating or maintaining any Instagram accounts in violation of the Terms; (c) engaging in any

                                   9   activity that violates the Terms or facilitating others to do the same; (d) soliciting third parties to

                                  10   access Meta’s platforms and computer systems on Defendants’ behalf; (e) engaging in any activity

                                  11   that disrupts, diminishes the quality of, interferes with the performance of, or impairs the

                                  12   functionality of Meta’s services, platforms, and computer systems; and (f) engaging in activity that
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   violates Section 502. See Compl. at 17–18 (Request for Relief).

                                  14           To obtain permanent injunctive relief, “[a] plaintiff must demonstrate: (1) that it has

                                  15   suffered an irreparable injury; (2) that remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are

                                  16   inadequate to compensate for that injury; (3) that, considering the balance of hardships between

                                  17   the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted; and (4) that the public interest would

                                  18   not be disserved by a permanent injunction.” eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388,

                                  19   391 (2006). The Court has discretion to grant or deny permanent injunctive relief. Id. The

                                  20   undersigned finds these factors, on balance, support issuing a permanent injunction.

                                  21                   a.      Irreparable Injury
                                  22           “Numerous courts have found that unauthorized access of computers and the acquisition of

                                  23   data . . . constitute[s] irreparable harm.” Facebook, Inc. Power Ventures, 252 F. Supp. 3d 765,

                                  24   782 (N.D. Cal. 2017), aff’d, 749 F. App’x 557 (9th Cir. 2019). And “[i]rreparable harm may be

                                  25   established where there is the fact of an injury, such as that arising from a breach of contract, but

                                  26   where there is an inability to ascertain the amount of damage” attributable to, for example, “[t]he

                                  27   threat to Plaintiff’s business.” Optronic Techs., Inc. v. Ningbo Sunny Elec. Co., Ltd., 2020 WL

                                  28   1812257, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 9, 2020), aff’d, 20 F.4th 466 (9th Cir. 2021). Here, Defendants’
                                                                                          15
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL           Document 18        Filed 08/01/25        Page 16 of 18




                                   1   continued access and use of Instagram to promote their unauthorized services after Meta sent a

                                   2   cease-and-desist letter and revoked their access to Instagram gives rise to irreparable injury.

                                   3   Compl. ¶¶ 28–45. Meta has suffered—and continues to suffer—irreparable harm to its reputation

                                   4   and goodwill as a result of Defendants’ unauthorized access and use of Meta’s platform that

                                   5   monetary damages cannot rectify. Stuhlbarg Int’l Sales Co. v. John D. Brush & Co., 240 F.3d

                                   6   832, 841 (9th Cir. 2001) (“Evidence of threatened loss of prospective customers or goodwill

                                   7   certainly supports a finding of the possibility of irreparable harm.”).

                                   8                  b.      Inadequacy of Monetary Damages
                                   9          As to the second factor, “not only has [Meta] suffered irreparable harm, it is very likely

                                  10   that in the absence of a permanent injunction, [Meta] will suffer irreparable harm again in the

                                  11   future.” Power Ventures, 252 F. Supp. 3d at 783. The undersigned notes that Defendants’ illicit

                                  12   conduct continued despite their receipt of Meta’s cease-and-desist letter. Compl. ¶¶ 40–45.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Absent an injunction, there is nothing to prevent Defendants from further attempts to access and

                                  14   use Meta’s platform and services without authorization. Monetary damages, therefore, are

                                  15   inadequate to compensate Meta’s injury. See Power Ventures, 252 F. Supp. 3d at 783 (money

                                  16   damages inadequate where “there is a reasonable likelihood of defendant’s future violations”)

                                  17   (quotations omitted); Sluchevsky, 2020 WL 5823277, at *9 (“Where defendants’ conduct indicates

                                  18   there is a ‘reasonable likelihood of defendant’s future violations,’ . . . and defendants retain the

                                  19   software, tools or means at issue to continue their harmful behavior, this moves eBay’s second

                                  20   factor in favor of granting a permanent injunction.”) (quoting Pyro Spectaculars N., Inc. v. Souza,

                                  21   861 F. Supp. 2d 1079, 1092 (E.D. Cal. 2012)). As such, the undersigned finds Meta has

                                  22   established that “remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are inadequate to

                                  23   compensate” for the harm it has suffered regarding its ability to prevent Defendants from further

                                  24   attempts to access and use its platform and services without authorization. eBay, 547 U.S. at 391.

                                  25                  c.      Balance of Hardships
                                  26          The balance of hardships also tips in Meta’s favor. Meta “has suffered harm because of

                                  27   Defendants’ illegal conduct, and absent a permanent injunction face the probability of Defendants

                                  28   again engaging in similar conduct. In contrast, a permanent injunction would only require
                                                                                         16
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01678-RFL           Document 18        Filed 08/01/25      Page 17 of 18




                                   1   Defendants to comply with the law. This balance, therefore, weighs in favor of granting a

                                   2   permanent injunction.” Sluchevsky, 2020 WL 5823277, at *9; Ates, 2023 WL 4035611, at *9

                                   3   (“Enjoining [defendants’] violation of the Instagram Terms of Use presents little to no hardship on

                                   4   [them].”); Nguyen, 2023 WL 8686924, at *11 (“In contrast, a permanent injunction would only

                                   5   require Defendants to comply with the law.”). On the other hand, Defendants forced Meta to incur

                                   6   costs to investigate and mitigate their repeated violations of the Terms. Defendants’ unauthorized

                                   7   access and use of Instagram to sell and provide unauthorized services warrants an injunction.

                                   8                  d.      Public Interest
                                   9          The public interest would be served by an injunction. Indeed, the public has a significant

                                  10   interest in enjoining a suspected abuser of Meta’s platform from accessing Meta’s products and

                                  11   distributing or monetizing any services constituting improper use of Meta’s products. See Stackla,

                                  12   Inc. v. Facebook, Inc., 2019 WL 4738288, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 27, 2019) (“[Meta]’s ability to
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   decisively police the integrity of its platform is without question a pressing public interest. In

                                  14   particular, the public has a strong interest in the integrity of [Meta]’s platforms, [Meta]’s policing

                                  15   of those platforms for abuses, and [Meta]’s protection of its users’ privacy.”); Sluchevsky, 2020

                                  16   WL 5823277, at *9. As such, the undersigned finds a permanent injunction would advance a

                                  17   cognizable public interest.

                                  18          In sum, the undersigned finds each of the factors supports granting a permanent injunction

                                  20   injunctive relief against Defendants.

                             1                                     III.         LEGAL STANDARD

                             2          Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 55(b)(2) permits a court, following default by a

                             3   defendant, to enter default judgment in a case. “The district court’s decision whether to enter

                             4   default judgment is a discretionary one.” Aldabe v. Aldabe, 616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980).

                             5          At the default judgment stage, the factual allegations of the complaint, except those

                             6   concerning damages, “together with other competent evidence submitted” are deemed admitted

                             7   by the non-responding parties. Shanghai Automation Instrument Co. v. Kuei, 194 F. Supp. 2d

                             8   995, 1000 (N.D. Cal. 2001); see also Fair Hous. of Marin v. Combs, 285 F.3d 899, 906 (9th Cir.

                             9   2002) (“With respect to the determination of liability and the default judgment itself, the general

                            10   rule is that well-pled allegations in the complaint regarding liability are deemed true.”).

                            11   “However, a defendant is not held to admit facts that are not well-pleaded or to admit
DAVIS WRIGHT TREMAINE LLP




                            12   conclusions of law.” DIRECTV, Inc. v. Hoa Huynh, 503 F.3d 847, 854 (9th Cir. 2007) (citation

                            13   and quotation omitted). Therefore, “necessary facts not contained in the pleadings, and claims

                            14   which are legally insufficient, are not established by default.” Cripps v. Life Ins. Co. of N. Am.,

                            15   980 F.2d 1261, 1267 (9th Cir. 1992) (citing Danning v. Lavine, 572 F.2d 1386, 1388 (9th Cir.

                            16   1978)); accord DIRECTV, 503 F.3d at 854. Further, the scope of relief is limited by Federal

                            17   Rule of Civil Procedure 54(c), which states that a “default judgment must not differ in kind from,

                            18   or exceed in amount, what is demanded in the pleadings.”

                            19          In determining whether default judgment is appropriate, the Ninth Circuit enumerated the

                            20   following factors for courts to consider:

                            21          (1) the possibility of prejudice to plaintiff, (2) the merits of plaintiff’s substantive
                                        claim, (3) the sufficiency of the complaint, (4) the sum of money at stake in the
                            22          action[,] (5) the possibility of a dispute concerning material facts[,] (6) whether
                                        the default was due to excusable neglect, and (7) the strong policy underlying the
                            23          Federal Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on the merits.
                            24   Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471–72 (9th Cir. 1986).
